questions.q: State the differential rate law for a zero order reaction and write the integrated rate equation obtained after integration with the initial condition \([R]_0\) at \(t=0\).
questions.a: The differential rate law is \(-\frac{d[R]}{dt} = k\). Integrating gives \([R] = -kt + [R]_0\). A wrong answer (e.g., writing \([R] = [R]_0 e^{-kt}\) or forgetting the negative sign) reveals confusion between zero and first order integrated forms or a sign error in the integration step.

questions.q: Explain why the plot of concentration \([R]\) versus time \(t\) for a zero order reaction is a straight line, and identify the physical meaning of its slope and intercept.
questions.a: The integrated equation \([R] = -kt + [R]_0\) is of the form \(y = mx + c\) with \(y = [R]\), \(x = t\), slope \(m = -k\), and intercept \(c = [R]_0\). A wrong answer (e.g., saying slope = \(k\) or intercept = 0) shows the student has not compared the equation to the straight-line form or has missed the negative sign in the slope.

questions.q: The decomposition of NH₃ on a platinum surface is a zero order reaction with \(k = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. If the initial concentration of NH₃ is 0.10 mol L⁻¹, calculate the concentration after 100 seconds.
questions.a: Using \([R] = [R]_0 - kt\): \([R] = 0.10 - (2.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 100) = 0.10 - 0.025 = 0.075\) mol L⁻¹. A wrong answer (e.g., 0.125 or using first order formula) indicates the student either added instead of subtracted, used the wrong integrated equation, or mishandled units.

questions.q: A student plots \([R]\) vs \(t\) for a zero order reaction and obtains a straight line with slope \(-3.2 \times 10^{-3}\) mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ and intercept 0.50 mol L⁻¹. Write the integrated rate equation for this reaction and predict the time when \([R]\) becomes 0.10 mol L⁻¹.
questions.a: Equation: \([R] = -3.2 \times 10^{-3} t + 0.50\). Set \([R] = 0.10\): \(0.10 = -3.2 \times 10^{-3} t + 0.50 \Rightarrow t = \frac{0.40}{3.2 \times 10^{-3}} = 125\) s. A wrong answer (e.g., using positive slope or solving incorrectly) shows inability to extract parameters from the graph or algebraic manipulation errors.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "For a zero order reaction, the half-life is independent of the initial concentration." Justify your answer using the integrated rate equation.
questions.a: The statement is FALSE. For zero order, \(t_{1/2} = \frac{[R]_0}{2k}\), which is directly proportional to \([R]_0\). A student who says "true" is confusing zero order with first order (where \(t_{1/2}\) is constant). This reveals a lack of derivation of half-life from the integrated equation.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment (using concentration vs time data) to confirm that the decomposition of N₂O₅ in CCl₄ is NOT a zero order reaction. Describe what you would plot and what result would disprove zero order kinetics.
questions.a: Plot \([N_2O_5]\) vs \(t\). If the reaction were zero order, the plot would be linear. Since N₂O₅ decomposition is first order, the plot will be a curve (exponential decay). A linear \(\ln[N_2O_5]\) vs \(t\) plot would confirm first order. A poor answer (e.g., plotting rate vs concentration) shows misunderstanding of how integrated rate equations are used to determine order.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: For a zero order reaction, the rate of reaction is independent of the ______ of the reactant(s).

Fill in the blank: Imagine a catalytic converter in a car exhaust: the ______ of ammonia on a hot platinum surface proceeds at a constant rate regardless of how much ammonia is left, because the platinum surface becomes saturated.
